newsitem.title: USA: Juror excused in Oklahoma City bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: Juror excused in Oklahoma City bombing trial.

text.p: Federal Judge Richard Matsch Tuesday excused a potential juror from serving in the Oklahoma City bombing trial, saying he did not believe she could be impartial.

The woman, a German-born naturalised U.S. citizen in her late 50s, had written in a questionnaire that she disagreed with Matsch's decision to move the trial from Oklahoma to Denver to ensure defendant Timothy McVeigh a fair hearing.

The three-times divorced woman, who said she was physically abused by two husbands, also said she suffered from high blood pressure and feared the stress of a high-profile trial might affect her health.

"I excused the previous juror based principally on her answers in the questionnaire and the determination that she could not serve as a fair and impartial juror in this case," Matsch said on the seventh day of the trial.

She was only the second of 38 potential jurors questioned so far to be immediately and publicly excused from jury duty in the trial of McVeigh, who is accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in April 1995, killing 168 people.
The identity of the potential jurors is kept secret and they sit behind a wooden panel in the courtroom.
One woman was dismissed last week because she had been treated for stress and feared breaking down.

Matsch is meeting daily with prosecutors and defence attorneys to discuss which of the other potential jurors to remove for reasons such as opposition to the death penalty or economic hardship. These decisions have not been made public.

The woman excused on Tuesday came to the United States in 1957 after marrying an American soldier. She wrote in a 40-page questionnaire last month that she strongly disagreed with moving the trial to Denver and thought the U.S. legal system was too protective of defendants' rights.

Matsch decided in February 1996 to move the trial because of fears McVeigh and co-defendant Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately, could not receive a fair trial anywhere in Oklahoma because of the impact of the bombing.

The woman also wrote that it was difficult for her to accept the events in Oklahoma City given her experience as a child in Germany during the Second World War. After briefly questioning her, Matsch lectured her on the U.S. Constitution and the guarantee of a fair trial.
Matsch asked if she disagreed with the principle that a person cannot be convicted without due process of law. "That depends on the way the law is put and how the law is practiced," the woman said.
Another potential juror said she could set aside news accounts of the bombing. "I know there are a lot of missing pieces out there."

The woman, who works in retailing, criticised government tax policy, saying it was becoming harder to raise a family. "I think we're getting close to the issue that started the (American) Revolution," she said.

She also said she believed the U.S. government was at times too intrusive. Attorneys are probing potential jurors' opinions on a wide range of subjects including the death penalty and attitudes toward the federal government.
